## 1. What was read

**745 research articles** from 33 of the 33 journals on the roster.

A further **176** records (19% of the 921 this month's harvest returned) carry no abstract and are not research: news, correspondence, editor highlights and obituaries. PubMed types them `Journal Article` and nothing else, so the publication-type filter cannot see them — across the whole index they are 22.7% of it and 35% of `general`, and 3,801 of them are JAMA. !!! warning "Volume swing against the median month: cancer -28%"
    Check the source before reading anything into this. Two benign causes account for most of these. `bioinfo` every January carries the Nucleic Acids Research database issue and runs high. And several journals simply deposit nothing in some months: across the 44 months read, 4 of 33 journals are absent from at least one, worst being *Nat Mach Intell* (20 months missing, 81 papers in total) and *Bioinformatics* (4 months missing, 2,905 papers in total). Every journal on the roster contributed this month. Queried directly, PubMed returns zero for those journal-months too — the holes are in the source, reproduced exactly by re-running the harvest. So a swing here is not evidence that a field went quiet, and is not usually evidence that the pipeline broke either.

Largest contributors: Nature 106, Nucleic Acids Res 98, JAMA 90, Science 79, Bioinformatics 66, Cell 41.

## 3. The evidence that moved it






**A clinical-AI null with the detail to be acted on.** [38965432](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38965432/) (*Nat Med*)
builds a dataset of 2,400 real patient cases from MIMIC across four common
abdominal pathologies, and a framework that makes a model work the way a
clinician does — gather the information, order the tests, reach a diagnosis
inside a workflow — rather than answer exam questions. State-of-the-art large
language models diagnose significantly worse than physicians across all four
pathologies, follow neither diagnostic nor treatment guidelines, and cannot
interpret laboratory results. They also fail to follow instructions and are
sensitive to both the quantity and the order of the information they are given,
which is why the authors say they cannot simply be dropped into existing
workflows. The paper's own conclusion is that these models are "not ready for
autonomous clinical decision-making". This is a refutation on `foundation-models`
of a kind the thread rarely gets: not a benchmark score but a named failure on
each of the things a deployment would need.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    The claim and this paragraph both carried a date argument — that the
    clinical-AI counterweight this corpus had placed in mid-2025 was in the
    flagship venue in September 2024. `threads.yml` already supersedes it:
    *Nature Medicine* states clinical-AI limitations in titles in 2023-10 and
    again in 2023-12. The right fix is not a new date but no date. The finding
    above needs none to carry it, and the stance is unchanged.

## 4. Refutations

### (a) Landing on a tracked thread

The month's one thread-level refutation is the clinical decision-making paper
described in section 3, filed on `foundation-models` and left there rather than
repeated here. Nothing else lands. September 2024 is the quietest month in the
2024 half of the corpus for thread-relevant refutations, and since 2024 was read
thread-first rather than exhaustively, that should be read as a limit on the
reading rather than a fact about the month.

### (b) Method credibility

[39322959](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39322959/) (*Genome Biol*): a realistic benchmark for differential-abundance
testing **and confounder adjustment** in human microbiome studies — the direct
methodological successor to May's *Nature Medicine* confounders paper, four
months later, and evidence that the objection was taken up rather than absorbed.

[39227979](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39227979/): a multiple-imputation procedure **outperforms** complete-case
and single imputation in differential expression. The default handling of missing
data in the standard pipeline is wrong.

[39152037](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39152037/) (*Genome Res*) proposes the smallest change to standard
sequence alignment that would let a search sum the probabilities of alternative
alignments instead of scoring one: it makes chance similarity easier to judge,
finds distant relationships that single-alignment scoring misses, and costs
almost nothing in run time. A single-author methods paper, carried here as a note
rather than as a ledger entry.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    This entry read: "Simple-beats-complex again, and this is the third instance
    in 2024 alone — January's linear brain dynamics, March's convolutions,
    September's alignment probabilities. A genre this corpus first recorded as a
    2026 phenomenon is running at roughly one paper a quarter in 2024." The word
    "simple" in a title was matched to a motif the corpus likes. The paper
    examines no published tool and reports no adverse finding, so it is not an
    audit and its stance is now `neutral`. The chain it anchored has also lost
    its January link: the linear-brain-dynamics paper was removed from
    `foundation-models` on the same grounds, that a shared slogan is not a shared
    result. Counting a genre by matching adjectives across titles produced a
    trend out of three unrelated papers.
